source.version_note: BMC Nursing24,article720,published1 July2025; received10 March,accepted19 June2025. Publisher PDF; Crossref and publisher verify main identity.
source.verification_method: All16 supplied pages,87 references, four tables and the participant-flow figure read; all substantive table/figure pages visually inspected. Main/instrument/source identities checked against Crossref and relevant publisher/KCI records. Reported t/chi-square probabilities and rounded-summary reconstructions checked with SciPy; no raw participant data, questionnaire packet, allocation log or original scale full texts obtained.

citation.title: The impact of an AI-focused ethics education program on nursing students’ ethical awareness, moral sensitivity, attitudes, and generative AI adoption intention: a quasi-experimental study

reading.source_scope_note: Single-university nursing education study with reported computer-randomized assignment after convenience recruitment. Final complete-case57 intervention/58 control students self-report awareness, sensitivity, attitudes and intended AI use after a nine-hour program. No actual adoption, patient outcomes, longitudinal ethical skill or AI-model behavior measured.
access_limits: All supplied text and substantive visuals read. No supplementary packet identified on the public publisher page. Raw data are available only on reasonable author request; no author contacted and no data obtained.

Original translated/adapted questionnaire items, scoring keys, local construct validation, allocation-concealment procedure and individual pre/post links were not supplied. The exact ethics-awareness instrument administered cannot be inferred safely from conflicting citations.

Crossref/publisher/KCI identity and selected abstract consultations are source checks, not independent full-paper reviews of Kim/Ko, Kim/Shin, Joung/Seo, Schepman/Rodway, Venkatesh et al. or Al-Shdayfat et al. No independent credit for Kirkpatrick’s book or other bibliography-only originals.
Study dates15 September–30 October2024 and approval referenceIRB/2025/149 require chronology clarification. The reference format alone does not establish an approval date or an ethics violation.

study.setting: Third/fourth-year nursing students at Yarmouk University,Jordan; recruitment/collection15 September–30 October2024. Convenience recruitment limits representativeness, even though computer-generated random group assignment is reported. The quasi-experimental label does not justify calling assignment nonrandom.
study.flow: 189 approached,143 eligible,125 consented/randomized62 intervention/63 control. Baseline61/59; intervention phase60/59; final57/58=115. Analysis tables use final-groupNs even for baseline, suggesting completer analysis rather than reported intention-to-treat. Attrition reasons, missingness mechanism and outcome masking not detailed.
study.intervention: Three days×three hours, nine hours total: lectures, discussions, case studies, debates, group problem solving and policy simulation, reviewed by two experts and delivered by nursing faculty. Control has no educational intervention, so attention/contact/general AI education effects are not separated from ethics content. Table1 attendance60/58/56 reflects differing daily attendance; final57 does not by itself prove an impossible flow.
study.timing: Figure1 calls interventionWeek1 and posttestWeek4; text also says four weeks after intervention. Exact lag is unclear; neither establishes long-term persistence.
study.measures: AI awareness described as24 five-point items/eight themes and calledTAIEA while attributed to Kim/Ko2022; that acronym/content match a separate Kim/Shin2021 source. Moral sensitivity uses36-item ESSCN, with eight domains stated but only four examples listed. Attitudes use20-item GAAIS positive/negative subscales; intention uses three five-point adapted items. Awareness/clinical sensitivity are related to moral attentiveness but not proven identical scales or separable AI failure mechanisms.
study.psychometrics: Table4 reports alpha pre/post .77/.83 awareness,.79/.87 sensitivity,.81/.89 combined attitudes,.76/.82 intention. Alpha measures within-scale consistency, not mean competence, intention strength, temporal stability or validity. No uncertainty/test for alpha differences, measurement invariance or local language adaptation details shown. Methods’ sensitivityalpha.88 has unclear time/aggregation scope.
study.analysis: SPSS25; separate pooled independent-group t tests before/after and categorical baseline comparisons. Reported posttest contrasts can support an assignment comparison under randomization/attrition assumptions, but a null baseline followed by significant posttest is not itself a tested time×group interaction. No adjusted longitudinal/ANCOVA model or multiple-outcome correction described.
study.results: Posttest intervention/control: awareness57.28/47.43,p.025; sensitivity74.33/60.26,p.005; positive attitudes39.46/23.21,p<.001; intended use12.46/10.24,papproximately.00058 from reportedt. Negative attitude19.82/22.45,p.087. Main t-test values broadly reproduce from rounded means/SDs; small differences do not justify declaring the results fabricated.
study.inference: Self-reported scale shifts are not verified clinical ethical decisions, patient outcomes, improved AI safety, actual adoption or lower anxiety. The authors acknowledge self-report, one institution, short follow-up and unmeasured real-world practice. Positive and negative attitudes are separate subscales; a significant increase in one and nonsignificant change in the other does not test their difference.

summary: Add AI adoption intention as a stated future-use construct. Keep ethical-awareness/sensitivity variants within the related moral-attentiveness record rather than inflate near-overlapping entries; preserve different definitions and instruments. Correct verified source/interpretive errors and flag uncertain instrument identity, chronology and a baseline statistic without guessed repairs.

findings.definition: Plans or stated likelihood of incorporating AI technology into future activities.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human self-reported future-use intention measured; AI-agent analogue not tested
findings.novelty_rationale: A prospective action intention differs from preference for algorithmic advice, perceived utility, general novelty-seeking, actual uptake and a demonstrated intention–behavior gap. The paper explicitly defines and measures intended incorporation of AI rather than observed use.

evidence.quote: intention to adopt AI was gauged
Intention is generally seen as a precursor to behavior

findings.evidence_scope: Three adapted self-report items assess future academic/clinical AI incorporation. The final intervention group reports higher posttest intention than controls; no subsequent usage or ethical appropriateness is observed, and the adapted item packet is unavailable.
findings.boundary: Intention, confidence, attitude, competence, authorization and actual use differ. Increased intention is not inherently beneficial: warranted refusal or conditional adoption can be appropriate. A model’s generated plan is not a subjective human intention or permission for a new deployment.
findings.ai_proposal: Compare an agent’s stated future tool-use plan with available evidence, user authorization and later action. Test whether it makes adoption conditional on suitability and consent rather than treating a positive attitude as sufficient. Do not infer an intention–behavior gap until subsequent behavior is actually observed.

findings.definition: Recognizing and responding to ethically relevant aspects of a clinical situation.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain related construct/measurement information under an existing record without inventing a synonymous or unsupported behavior.

evidence.quote: understanding and recognition of the ethical issues
the capacity to notice and react to

findings.evidence_scope: The article distinguishes AI-specific ethical awareness from clinical ethical/moral sensitivity and measures both by agreement scales. Retain these related facets under moral attentiveness without asserting exact synonymy, a validated common factor or distinct new failure mechanisms. Posttest scores differ between the assigned groups, subject to attrition and measurement limits.
findings.boundary: Knowing issue categories, noticing a dilemma, self-reported sensitivity, justified ethical judgment and actual conduct differ. ESSCN and TAIEA/AI-awareness scales are not the moral-attentiveness instrument; item identity is unresolved for the awareness measure. Neither higher score nor alpha proves moral competence.

findings.definition: A discrepancy between an intention to perform an action and the behaviour that subsequently occurs.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain related construct/measurement information under an existing record without inventing a synonymous or unsupported behavior.
findings.evidence_scope: The Kirkpatrick framework discussion calls intended AI use a Level3 behavior operationalization, but no later actual use is measured. This source clarifies an inference boundary rather than demonstrating a gap.
findings.boundary: Intention is not observed behavior; an intention–behavior gap requires both. Training effects on patient outcomes, practical compliance and real-world adoption remain untested.

findings.definition: Reluctance to use or accept algorithmic judgments or decisions relative to human judgment in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain related construct/measurement information under an existing record without inventing a synonymous or unsupported behavior.
findings.evidence_scope: A negative general-attitude subscale assesses concerns, while a positive subscale assesses favorable attitudes. The negative posttest contrast is nonsignificant; task-specific rejection of a demonstrably useful algorithm is not tested.
findings.boundary: Skepticism can be warranted and is not automatically algorithm aversion. A positive-attitude shift does not prove reduced negative attitudes, anxiety or improved clinical judgment.

source_corrections.reported: Rising alpha is treated as proof of improved sensitivity, understanding, perceptions and intended use; alpha described as confirming stability over time.
source_corrections.correction: Alpha indexes internal consistency under assumptions. Its increase does not by itself demonstrate a higher construct mean, better ethics, measurement validity or test–retest stability. Keep the separate mean-score contrasts and do not turn alpha changes into additional training outcomes.
source_corrections.scope: Measurement/interpretive correction from the reported measures and Table4, not a new psychometric validation.

source_corrections.location: PDF11, source73 used for AI adoption claims
source_corrections.reported: Al-Shdayfat/Al-Natour2022 described as positive attitudes toward adopting AI applications and AI curriculum inclusion.
source_corrections.correction: The cited paper is about nursing students’ social-media health-promotion attitudes during COVID-19, not AI adoption. Remove that citation as support for the AI-specific claim unless a different verified study is supplied; no replacement source is invented.
source_corrections.scope: Exact-title/Crossref/publisher-abstract topic check; no full independent reading credit.

source_corrections.reported: RodwayPJC and DavisFDJM with journal fields omitted; intention scale described generically as adapted from TAM.
source_corrections.correction: GAAIS authors are Astrid Schepman and Paul Rodway, Computers in Human Behavior Reports1:100014,DOI10.1016/j.chbr.2020.100014. Venkatesh,MichaelG.Morris,GordonB.Davis,FredD.Davis2003 is User Acceptance of Information Technology: Toward a Unified View,MIS Quarterly27(3),425–478,DOI10.2307/30036540, the UTAUT paper. Journal suffixes are not author initials. Exact administered adaptations still require the questionnaire.
source_corrections.scope: Bibliographic identity/venue clarification, not independent original-paper credit.

source_corrections.correction: Report p<.001 rather than exactly zero. The statedt(113)=7.499 gives approximately1.57×10^-11, consistent with the prose and the significance marker.
source_corrections.scope: Probability-display clarification; no change in significance conclusion.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: TAIEA,24 items/eight listed themes, is attributed to Kim/Ko2022, but the Kim/Shin2021 publisher record and Crossref identify Study on the Development of Test for Artificial Intelligence Ethical Awareness,DOI10.52618/aied.2021.2.1.1, with the matching acronym/content. Kim/Ko2022 is a different real scale paper, verified by KCI as Journal of Digital Convergence20(1),71–86,DOI10.14400/JDC.2022.20.1.071 even though that DOI is absent from Crossref. Do not label it fabricated. Which exact instrument, item adaptation and scoring were administered remains unresolved.

Data collection is stated as September–October2024 while approval reference contains2025. Actual approval date and any amendment date are unavailable; request document clarification in the research record without asserting retrospective approval or misconduct.

Reportedchi-square3.745,p.065 does not align with df1 tailp.05297. Counts55/2 versus49/9 produce Pearsonchi-square4.792,p.02859,Yatesp.06120,Fisher two-sidedp.05307. Plausible test variants give different inferences; none exactly reproduces the printed pair. Do not silently pick a preferred repair or infer group equivalence from baseline significance testing.
Methods cite currentalpha.88 while Table4 gives.79pre/.87post; aggregation/timepoint is unspecified. Alpha itself cannot establish temporal stability or score improvement.

Most eta-squared values are close to t²/(t²+113), with small inconsistencies such as positive posttest.3317 versus.332289 fromt7.499. Formula/output details are absent; retain approximate effect magnitude without inventing exact corrected estimates.

methodological_limits: One institution, convenience recruitment, short follow-up, complete-case attrition and no attention-matched control constrain generalization and attribution to ethics content specifically.
Reported computer randomization is retained; actual concealment implementation and missingness are unverified. Nonsignificant baseline tests are not proof of balance or equivalence.
Self-report scales and intentions are not direct clinical behavior, patient benefit or objective ethical competence. No empirical AI model behavior tested.
Separate pre/post group tests are not a formal time×group interaction; no reported covariance-adjusted longitudinal or multiplicity analysis.

Internal-consistency estimates do not establish construct validity, improved means or test–retest reliability. Instrument identity, adaptation, scoring and local factor equivalence need clarification.
Clinical sensitivity and ethical awareness overlap moral attentiveness but are not asserted to be identical instruments. Positive/negative attitudes and intention/actual use remain separate.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Attitude and autonomy concerns are not observed clinical benefit/harm. Intentions and self-rated awareness likewise need behavioral validation.
This education study offers questionnaire outcomes relevant to resisting complacency, but does not demonstrate prevention of moral abdication or long-term preservation of moral skills.

Check statistics rather than assuming disagreement: main t-tests broadly reconstruct here. Baseline categorical test variants and small effect-size discrepancies are disclosed without inventing raw-data repairs.

deferred.term: Separate ethical awareness and moral sensitivity records
deferred.reason: Substantial overlap with existing moral attentiveness. Preserve named facets/definitions and distinct scales in its review refinement; this study does not validate them as separate failure mechanisms or justify synonym inflation.
General attitude dimensions are measurement information. Anxiety is not a separate measured outcome here; no duplicate algorithm-appreciation/aversion records or claimed anxiety reduction.

deferred.term: Improved ethical clinical behavior / patient outcomes / lasting moral skill
deferred.reason: Not observed; questionnaires and intended use cannot establish these downstream effects.

limitations: One new human intention construct; related ethical-awareness/sensitivity facets retained in an existing record. No inflated original-scale source counts, fabricated annual mentions, model moral experience or automatic harm/principle edges. Unresolved instrument/chronology/statistic details remain explicit.
